transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well... my wife wanted me to come in. She gets pretty frustrated with me lately. She'll be telling me about, you know, my cousin's appointments or who's giving him rides... and I'm looking right at her, listening, I think. But then a minute later I realize I didn't actually take in half of what she said. So... here I am.

When you're doing things you really enjoy or find interesting—like watching a show you like or a hobby—do you have trouble paying attention in those situations too, or is it mainly when your wife is talking to you about everyday things?

It's not just with her. I mean... if I'm trying to figure out a catering order, or I'm on one of those planning calls for the parish... I'll start out okay. But then... I don't know, my mind just goes somewhere else. I end up having to read the same notes over again because it's like I never even looked at them. So, yeah. It happens then, too.

When you're doing something you really enjoy—like watching your favorite TV show or working on a hobby you love—do you find it easy to focus and stay with it, or do you have trouble concentrating even then?

Well... I guess if it's something I really like doing... I don't really know. I haven't paid much attention to that. I suppose I watch TV fine, mostly. I don't really have a lot of hobbies right now. So... I'm not really sure.
Besides having trouble focusing, do you find yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or like you need to move around a lot? Or do you act without thinking things through first?
No... not really. I don't feel restless or anything like that. I mostly just sit. And I don't think I do things without thinking. I'm just... easily distracted, I guess. That's about it.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F98.8 (other specified behavioral and emotional disorders) and F06.8 (other specified mental disorders due to known physiological condition) because patient denies hyperactivity, restlessness, impulsivity, and acting without thinking. Symptoms are consistent with inattentive-type ADHD (predominantly inattentive presentation) without hyperactive-impulsive features. Patient reports persistent difficulty sustaining attention across multiple contexts (conversation, work tasks, reading) without evidence of secondary medical causes or behavioral/emotional disorder features.
